utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone else in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel and Muriel Cauvin legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Friday I bid good afternoon all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused and all those in and around the courtroom. We are starting with a few minutes' delay due to technical problems which have fortunately been resolved. On the programme today we have a witness who should be brought in and without further ado, I would like to ask the usher to bring in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Let me check that you are hearing the interpretation of my words in your own language. If that is the case, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a witness of the Defence. Before taking the solemn declaration, I need to know your identity to know who is going to testify, and that is why I ask you to tell me your first and last name, date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm Mirsad Mesic, born on the 30th of March, 1971 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are you currently engaged in an occupation? If so, which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a teacher by profession, but I'm currently employed in my own privately owned company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, 1993, did you have a position or an occupation? If so, which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in 1992, I was employed at Zenica municipality as commander of the Municipal Staff of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you, sir, already testified about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993 either in an international or a domestic court, or is this the first time for you to testify in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did have occasion to speak to your investigators about 1995 or 1996, and that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Will you now read the solemn declaration which the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Defence counsel, as I do in the case of all witnesses, I provide some explanation to them as to the way in which the proceedings will evolve so that you can understand what is going to happen and also to ensure the smooth running of this hearing. Regarding what is going to happen, you will have to answer questions which will be put to you first by the attorneys representing the accused, whom you have already met, and they are seated to your left. Usually we plan an hour or an hour and a half for questions coming from the Defence. And also, the attorneys for the second accused may have questions for you. At the end of this stage, which in our procedure is known as the examination-in-chief of the Defence witness, the Prosecution will also have questions for you within the framework of what is known as the cross-examination. The Prosecution is seated to your right. There are two gentlemen, but only one of them will be asking you questions. And normally the Prosecution has the same amount of time for questions as the Defence. Upon the termination of that stage, the Defence counsel may have additional questions for you, which will be linked to the answers which you provided to the questions during the cross-examination. The three Judges seated in front of you may at any point in time ask you questions, but they prefer, in the interest of the good management of the proceedings, for the parties to complete their questions, and when all those questions have been answered satisfactorily, the Judges need not necessarily ask you any questions. However, if they need to clarify certain answers given to either party or if they feel that your answers have a certain number of shortcomings, which in the interest of justice and truth and need further clarification, therefore the Judges will have questions for you. You will note that the questions of each party may differ. Do your best to answer those questions clearly, because, sir, you must know that as far as you are concerned and your testimony, we have nothing in writing. We don't know who you are, what exactly you're going to testify about. It is only the oral answers to the questions which will allow us, the Judges to have the best possible understanding of what you yourself saw or can testify about. During the questions, the parties, and possibly the Judges, may show you documents, and you will be able to see those documents in your own languages, and we will hear your comments about them. I also need to inform you of two other points which are important and which it is my duty to refer to for the benefit of all witnesses. Witnesses have duties and rights. The principal duty that you have is to tell the truth as you have solemnly pledged to tell the whole truth. As you know, false testimony is an offence which is sanctioned in all countries, including this Tribunal. Therefore, false testimony in this Tribunal could lead to sanctions. The second point which is linked to our procedure in this Tribunal is that there is a possibility that an answer to a particular question might at some point in time be used against you. In that case, you may refuse to answer. But should that happen, and this is very rare, the Chamber may instruct you to answer the question nevertheless, and we guarantee you immunity from prosecution, which means that what you say in this Tribunal cannot be used against you one day. This is a provision of our Rules of Procedure so as to enable the establishment of the truth. These are all the points that it is my duty to remind you of. Should a question appear to you to be too complicated or too long, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. Should there be any difficulties, do not hesitate to let us know. It is now half past two. We will have a break in an hour and one-quarter, because for technical reasons we have to have breaks every Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond one and a half hours, which will give you the opportunity to take a rest for about 20 minutes, because as you will see, answering questions non-stop can be quite tiring. That is why a break will give you a chance to take a breather and to face the second part of the sitting after the break. Normally we continue until 7.00 p.m., so there will be two breaks for you to rest. So in total, you will have one hour of rest. I now give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the important instructions that you have just received from the president of the Trial Chamber, I should like to ask you something else. Both of us speak the same language, and as soon as I put my question to you, you could answer it promptly. However, both my question and your answers need to be interpreted so that the Trial Chamber and our colleagues in the courtroom are able to follow. That is why when I put my question to you, wait a moment before you answer it.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to a question from the president of the Trial Chamber, you said you were now living in Zenica. Mr. Mesic, where were you residing in April 1992 when the JNA and Serb forces attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I was living and working at the time in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you were a teacher. Could you tell us a little more about your education and where you acquired it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary and secondary school in Zenica, and I graduated from the Faculty of Political Sciences in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, before the war did you do your military service, in which army, and if you did serve, did you aware a rank?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I served in the Yugoslav People's Army. I completed the reserve officer school, and in 1992 I had the rank of reserve captain first class of the engineers. So I was an officer in reserve.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. Mesic, what was your occupation before the war and what jobs you held and for how long.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: From -- since 1976, I have been employed in the municipal Secretariat for National Defence in Zenica, and I started from an apprentice right up the scale. In 1992, I was acting secretary for national defence, and when the war started, I was the commander of the municipal civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your professional duties, do you know which document regulated the citizens' duties in defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Those obligations were regulated in the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and the law on defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the beginning of the war, did you know that Bosnia-Herzegovina passed its own law on defence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the day of its recognition, took over a series of laws from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this applied to the law on defence as well, which was taken over from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the situation was quite different from the one envisaged by the former SFRY, are you aware that in May 1992, Bosnia and Herzegovina passed its own law on defence and the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that, and I worked on the basis of those laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were the commander of the civilian protection in Zenica, what section of defence did civilian protection belong to? Was it part of the military or the civilian body of defence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: In my country and in all countries in the world, the civilian protection is a civilian body and deals with a set of measures and procedures to protect the civilian population and property from war devastation. So all these are civilian activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in 1992 and 1993, which was the superior body to the Municipal Staff of civilian protection in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: As soon as a state of war was declared, civilian protection came under the Crisis Staff, later the Presidency of the municipality, and these were the bodies who issued direct orders at the level of the municipality. And at the level of the republic, it was the republican staff of civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us briefly, Mr. Mesic, what were the main duties of civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: In simplified terms, it is a set of measures and activities to protect and save human lives and property from war devastation and, of course, natural disasters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To be able to fulfil those tasks, did the civilian protection have certain measures and instruments to perform the tasks entrusted to it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Of course. The civilian protection consisted of units and measures, staffs and commissioners. Units are quite clear, staffs are clear, and the measures were -- the activities were as follows: First aid, protection of animals, protection against unexploded mines, rescue from the rubble, and other activities. There are many.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, until when were you commander of the civilian staff in the civilian protection staff in the town of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: My involvement in the Zenica staff was until the end of March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the civilian protection come under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at any point in time or, rather, was the army at any point in time the superior body in relation to the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No. From contacts with colleagues in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I never heard of any such case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. Mesic, what was your relationship with units of the BH army? On what grounds were those relations built?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: One might say that those relations were relations of mutual respect and cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that you were given assignments first by the Crisis Staff and then the Presidency of Zenica municipality. Tell me whether pursuant to the law on defence you were a member of any civilian body as commander of the civilian protection staff for Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: According to the laws that you have referred to, the law on defence of Yugoslavia and later Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was ex officio member of the Crisis Staff and then member of the Presidency of Zenica municipality. These were bodies that performed the functions of the Municipal Assembly, and documents adopted at -- were to be verified at some future Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, in view of the tasks and measures that you listed a moment ago, tell me, what was the role in the civilian protection staff of professionals, qualified personnel?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: All measures that need to be implemented implied having professionals. So we had professionals for fire protection, veterinary surgeons, engineers for explosives, agricultural engineers, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the field, in local communes, in villages and hamlets, who performed civilian protection, and did these people -- did these people form a part of the system of civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: With the war, the activities were dispersed toward local communities, and they had bodies. They had executive bodies, they had staffs and a unit. In addition to them, there were commissioners whose task was to monitor the situation in the territory of the local commune to inform their staff about it and then of course, me too, that is the Municipal Staff, regarding any problems that may occur in the local communes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, let us clarify what you have just said. You said that the civilian authorities in local communes were formed and then also the staffs. As the word "staff" is very frequently mentioned when talking Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond about military bodies, when you said "staff," what did you mean, the staffs found in local communes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The terminology that we were using when -- was started -- came from the former system of All People's Defence. And according to that system, management of civilian defence bodies were entrusted to staffs and then there were units. But these have nothing to do with military organisations. But these names, these terms were actually taken over from the army. These were civilian bodies, nevertheless, and their duty was to ensure the functioning of civilian life, that is for civilians to be able to live normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in local communities, you had civilian protection staffs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of the numerous tasks and measures that you had to implement, tell me, please, was civilian -- did civilian protection carry out the sanitisation of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: One of the foremost roles of civilian protection was what we call asanacija, or sanitation, or clearing up the terrain, which means clearing up the area where a war was fought. It means picking up the bodies, burying the bodies, seeing to the corpses and the remainder of any livestock that might have been killed and any other consequences of the war such as putting out fires if any were started, and things like that, seeing to the destroyed houses, dealing with the rubble. Things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who performed this sanitisation of the terrain through an area where -- in an area where fighting had occurred?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The sanitisation of the terrain was a measure that the civilian protection organs dealt with in the area, and so in Zenica, it was the staff of the municipal of the civilian protection that was in charge of dealing with affairs of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the civilian protection staff, should the need arise, did they ask for assistance from other civilian organs to assist it as a reinforcement to help it carry out the tasks it was there to do?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Civilian protection had the task of seeing to the first -- the consequences of the initial impact of combat, and of course all the other organisations would help it out once conditions were right for that. So for example, in the case of refugees, the first wave of refugees was seen to by the Municipal Staff of civilian protection. They sorted their accommodation, prompt accommodation and food and all the rest of it, and then the municipal organs would step in to help out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, in view of the fact that we mentioned sanitisation of the terrain a moment ago, can we go to that, and can you remember whether towards the end of January, in an area of Zenica municipality, had there been any fighting, and did the staff of the civilian protection see to the sanitisation of that area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember in January 1993, for example, the Municipal Staff of civilian protection did conduct sanitisation in the area of the village of Dusina, and after the fighting and combat that had taken place in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you still happen to remember whether the Municipal Staff of civilian protection sent a team and who the members of the team were for it to conduct the sanitisation of the terrain after the fighting had been completed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Municipal Staff did send an expert team led by my assistant, and they saw to the sanitisation of the terrain after combat. And what else did you ask me? I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked whether anybody assisted you in tasks of that kind. You said it was your assistant. So who went with the team for the work to be done? Was there anybody else, any other organs or institutions or was any other equipment used? How did you transport the people or the corpses of people and animals and anything else that you needed to transport?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, in this case it was my assistant who went to deal with sanitisation with some helpers, and they were assisted by the local commune's organs of civilian protection. We always coordinated this work with the organs of internal affairs and the investigating organs of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember in that specific case, and generally speaking when you would undertake the sanitisation of a terrain, which organs supplied you with the first information that you were needed to go out into the field and conduct sanitisation? How did that information come to you? How were you informed about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Zenica in my opinion was a very well organised municipality, and it was capable of dealing with far more complex tasks than the present ones, and it was a system of monitoring the situation in the entire municipality, and this was called the service for observation and information, and it was tied in with the army and the police or rather cooperated with the army and police, and that was my operative organ supplying me with the first initial information as to what was to be done and where it was to be done. In this concrete case I received information from my commissioners via the centre for monitoring and information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After sanitisation of the terrain had been conducted, do you know where the bodies of those who were killed were transferred, transported?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: In my own town, anybody who was killed was taken to the hospital and a department there for storing corpses, that is to say the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this specific case was everybody transported to the hospital or were they all taken to the Zenica morgue or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, this particular event, and I don't want you to misunderstand me, but it was the standard type of work we had to deal with when people were killed. Zenica of -- there were many people in Zenica who were killed during the combats, whether through shelling or through fighting or anything of that kind, and we would always bury the dead according to the same principle. That is to say the bodies of those killed were taken to the city morgue. We organised the burials. We contacted family members and conducted the burial in the way that the families desired. And this would depend on whether they wanted -- which area of town they wanted their relatives to be buried in and what religious rites were to be observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, you said your assistant went and that he was in turn assisted by your commissioners in the field, on the spot. Once sanitisation had been taken care of, did any member of that team your assistant or anybody else, indicate to you or tell you that in that specific case in the field they had seen or come across or in other way informed of the fact that death had occurred in different ways, that is to say not in the usual way that death occurs during combat?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: According to the report from my assistant, all these casualties were the consequences of the fighting, of combat of the war. The bodies were found in different places, in different spots. They were collected together and taken to the city morgue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that you, as was your custom, would, once the analyses and investigation had been conducted, you would see to the burial of the people killed. Tell me, please, in the case of Dusina itself, did burials take place, and did any family members, that is to say the members of the families of the people killed, indicated that death might have been caused in some other way other than was reported to you by your team?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No. None of the people who contacted us discussed the cause of death or expressed any doubts with respect to the cause of death. And according to our standard practice, we buried the dead in the spots designated by them. For those who were not present, because after the combat, after the fighting a part of the population had withdrawn to the neighbouring municipality, which is just several hundred metres away from the place of action, we organised their burials in cooperation with the Catholic priest.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the village of Dusina and the whole Lasva Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond municipality, tell me, please, later on did your staff in that particular local commune or, rather, the commissioners, did they contact you and ask you questions about the protection of the property of persons who had left their houses?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, the protection of property is a separate question, and people always find it difficult to understand all the ramifications. If you -- if we remember New York in 1990 when there was no electricity, the consequences of that catastrophe were great. Some people were even killed. So people who thought they could solve their problems were in fact wrong, and the commissioners came to us to see how we were going to protect the property of those people, and a plan was adopted according to which all the property was to be recorded and placed in one space so that the people, when they came back, could reclaim their property, the property that they had left behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, may we now move on to a different period? Do you know whether in April 1993 there was any combat between the HVO and the BH army in Zenica? That is to say whether during that period of time there was a withdrawal of part of the HVO units and the Croats of Zenica from the town of Zenica itself?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to give you a broader answer to that question in view of the fact that I was a member of the Presidency at that point in time, and we had a enormous problem to deal with, that is to say the relationship between the HVO and the entire country's diverse [as interpreted] and the HVO, and life in Zenica in general. The HVO throughout its activities tried to obstruct the defence and to prepare for some kind of conflict which would ensure their supremacy in Zenica. The military units of the HVO did not go and fight the common enemy, the joint enemy, but they turned their positions focusing on Zenica, and the situation escalated, and they made it impossible to have any movement going on, and without very serious procedure you weren't able to travel 30 kilometres to the south or north of Zenica. So all the communes held by them had, in fact, been blocked, and any communication with the rest of the world was made impossible. We tried to discuss the situation with the representatives of the HVO on many occasions, because the HVO was a military and civilian authority as well. They were the same people. So you had to negotiate with those people. And we would talk to them often in the hope that we would come by a way of cooperating. But unfortunately, that -- we were not successful and the conflict broke out in April. It lasted for just one day, and it took place in several parts, and it was most intense in the northwestern regions of Zenica. In some other areas, the conflicts were not as great. Those people simply laid down their arms, so it didn't come to a fight at all, but that's what the conflict took place in those months of April -- those days of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you some more questions about that event I should like to ask you this: Something about the structure of the population in Zenica and the way in which the people of different ethnicities lived in the area before the war and at the beginning of the war too.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, the Zenica municipality on the basis of the 1991 population census, and I'm going to give you rough values, had -- 50 per cent of the population were Muslims, and that was what it was in Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Fifteen per cent were Croats, 15 per cent were Serbs, and about 20 per cent were others or the rest. They were people who referred to themselves and considered themselves to be Yugoslavs or some other ethnic group such as Albanians, Romany, and others. It was the life of an industrial town, and nobody jeopardised anybody on ethnic grounds or anything like that. People worked a lot. They earned a lot. The average salary was 1.000 German marks. They had free flats to live in, education for their children, and all the rest of it. There was a guaranteed religious freedom and all religious institutions which existed before the war continued to function during the war and after the war. Never at any point, and this is particularly true of Zenica, were there any, absolutely no national or ethnic tensions, nor was there any reason for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, tell me this, please. In view of the situation as it was before the war, in Zenica during the war did the organs of power and authority remain multi-ethnic in composition, and what about your Municipal Staff of civilian protection? What was the make-up of its members?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll be happy to. We entered the war with full respect for the national and ethnic make-up of -- on the basis of the 1991 population census, the set-up of the country at the time, and this was reflected in the Municipal Assembly and all the local organs of power and authority. They worked upon that principle and were founded upon that principle. The members of the Serbian Democratic Party stepped down from the positions of authority. At the time the army left our town, and they no longer participated in the local authorities and were replaced by some Serbs who lived in Zenica but were not members of the SDS party. Specifically speaking in my own staff, my deputy was a Serb from start to finish, until he tricked me and went over to the opposite side. But of course it was quite normal for all ethnic groups to be represented in the staff. So we had all the ethnic groups living in Zenica represented.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Their Honours know that the national parties won at the elections, and in view of the questions I'm now going to ask you and my desire to see how best to tackle this area, I'd like to ask you this: Did you ever begin to -- did you ever belong to any nationalist party?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I never belonged to a nationalist party, nor will I, for the simple reason that I do not think it's the right solution for my country.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And to bear that out, I see you have a badge which belongs to a multinational party in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't notice that, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now please tell me whether after the conflict, that is to say the conflict between the HVO and BH army in Zenica, did you as a help of the War Presidency and commander of the staff of civilian protection, were you given a specific assignment linked to the return of people who had left their homes during that period of time in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The work of the Croatian Democratic Community of the HVO in Zenica were geared towards, first and foremost, having Croats leave Zenica. This was also done by the Serbian Democratic Party. And the basic goal was ethnic cleansing of those two parties. As a consequence of the war and the fighting in Zenica, we saw an organised population movement under threat of force, and the inhabitants were moved out of their houses and moved away from their thresholds. And this resulted in complete chaos in which people without any desire to leave their homes did nonetheless leave their houses and apartments and took refuge in the forests in neighbouring municipalities and quite simply left their homes behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you continue, you said "on threat of force." Now, was that force exerted on them by the farm or the civilian police in Zenica? Which organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: There was organised pressure by the Croatian Defence Council via its activists in the local commune who had the uniform task of moving out the population in panic and fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. I'm sorry for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, the president of the municipality met every day to monitor and follow the security situation in the municipality and monitored all areas of life and work in the municipality, and they would take concrete measures aimed at ensuring safe and secure life, and in the extent possible a normal life in Zenica municipality, as much as that was possible. And in this specific case, too, the dual activities that took place, that is to say the population were encouraged to return. And the Presidency, on that same day, I think, if I'm correct, I'm not quite sure of the dates, of course, made a decision and passed an order to my staff which was given the task of having the Croatian population return to their homes. But what was not recorded in that particular document was the fact that we personally were in charge of that. That is to say I myself and Mr. Stjepan Radic, head of the church in -- the Catholic church in Zenica, the priest there. So we undertook this in a relatively short space of time, and we managed to have the population that had left returned to their homes. Now, the safety and security of those people was something that the regular police force saw to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I with like the usher's help now, please, to show some documents to the witness. It is a set of documents, in fact. Or, rather, just two documents. One is Prosecution Exhibit P371, and the second document is DH206. And I'd first of all like to ask the witness to take a look at P371, and number 1 in particular. One document is entitled "Conclusions," and the second is entitled "Order" or "Decree".

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, let's take a look at this first document dated the 18th of April. Is that the document you said was enacted the first day that the events took place in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document I meant. And my staff was bound to act in accordance with what these conclusions set out here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at the second document, the decree of the 26th of April, 1993. Is that, too, a document which refers to the tasks you described to us a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document. It is an authentic document. And if I might be allowed to add something?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: When I read through these documents I really do feel proud of what we were able to do during the war. I don't know that in the history of that unfortunate war in Bosnia-Herzegovina a single other municipality compiled a similar document. I'm talking about the municipalities on the Croatian and Serbian sides, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You said that most of the population returned to their homes. Now, the return of these people to their homes, did that in fact help you in your efforts, in your overall efforts to protect their property and to prevent any untoward activities that always accompany wars and conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Could you explain that, please? Could you ask me more simple terms?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You said that many people returned to their homes. What I would like to know now is this: To the best of your knowledge, the people who returned, were they sufficiently well-protected, and was their property protected from possible looting and destruction, the fact that they had returned?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, the basic meaning of the functioning of the Municipal Staff was to create normal or more normal conditions than conditions that prevailed during the war. The Croats and Serbs and Bosniaks lived in the same safety and security situations. They all faced the same problems, and nothing special or nothing separate happened to the Croats and Serbs than did to the Bosniaks. So the return of people provided security to the people who stayed on and was a good contribution to preventing the uncontrolled exodus of the population from Zenica. And in fact, not all the Croats or all the Serbs left Zenica, and I consider that to be a direct consequence of the activities undertaken by the municipal leadership and the staff which -- at whose head I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, tell me, please. You made significant efforts to have people return, people who left under different pressure and under different circumstances and who had left their homes temporarily. Now, tell me, were you an eyewitness of the arrival of people? Did you witness the arrival of people from other parts, coming into Zenica, and if so, how many people came in and what sort of problems did the civilian authorities have to face, including the civilian protection authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Before I answer that question, allow me to say, and I refer to the conflict in April 1993, that we had a lot of problems in bringing them back. In fact, the village of Grahovcici that is mentioned in this order, there was an attempt to prevent people returning in an organised manner by the HVO. Fortunately they did not succeed. And where people returned there was no problem with protection of the property. Protection of property was difficult in abandoned homes, because there's no way under conditions of total destitution that you can prevent looting in such cases. As for people coming to Zenica, I would like to suggest to you that I could refer to the aims behind this movement of the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, first, was there a movement of the population, and did a certain number of displaced and expelled people come to Zenica in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Zenica had 160.000 inhabitants before the war. The municipality of Zenica covers some 480 square kilometres, two-thirds of which is mountainous terrain. On such a small area, which was totally blocked by Serb and later Croat forces as well, a 100.000 new inhabitants arrived, people who had suffered the trauma that any normal man feels, thrown out of his house, witnessing execution and killings of his loved ones, a person who had lived normally, and suddenly he arrives in our town with absolutely nothing to his name. A man without any hope or any chances came to a town that had nothing to offer except goodwill to assist him. The environment was disastrously bad in terms of material facilities, but the people of Zenica did everything they could to make the stay of these people who had witnessed the worst possible atrocities. Can you imagine a person at a home watching television and suddenly being chased out of their homes without being allowed to take anything, first being looted, some members killed, and then they have to leave. So it was in those conditions that a hundred thousand new people arrive.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So please now look at document number 2. It is a special report of the head of the European monitoring commission, Ambassador Jean Pierre Tabeau. Tell me first whether Ambassador Tabeau in 1993 visited Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document is in English, and though my English is not too good, I would like to ask the interpreters to assist me so that the witness can tell me whether the description of these events in paragraph 2 of this document corresponds to what he personally experienced in 1993. "[In English] The situation is obviously extremely serious. Their number is rapidly increasing in April. Probably -- probably over 350.000 end of May, perhaps 400.000 with the ongoing effects of the Bosnian Serbs attacks in Brcko area and continuous expulsions from Banja Luka." [Interpretation] And now in the second paragraph it says: "[In English] 95 per cent of it was still covered in March, this has dramatically decreased in April to 15 per cent Tuzla still having 23 per cent, but Zenica receiving only 5 per cent (33 tons instead of 650) despite 33.000 refugees, 13 opstina representing 85.000 registered beneficiaries receiving nothing at all." [Interpretation] I apologise once again. I didn't have a Bosnian version of this text. What Ambassador Tabeau says here, that is that Zenica actually was receiving only 5 per cent of what it needed, does that reflect the situation as you saw it, as somebody living in Zenica at the time? Can you confirm this and describe it to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Even the figures given by Ambassador Tabeau reflect the disastrous situation in Zenica municipality and a shortage of everything. We didn't have food. We didn't have medical supplies. We didn't have power, fuel. We had people sick and dying as a result of expulsion. So I accept this fully, but I think that there were far more refugees than the Ambassador mentions here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mesic, in view of this dramatic situation in the municipality, did the Presidency of the municipality fully understand that the question of hunger, of not only the refugees but also the local population, could be of key significance for the safety of the people?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Let me say that I think that the question of hunger was one of the aims of the Serbian and Croat forces. It was a well-programmed and systematically implemented goal, and that was to bring a large number of refugees to Zenica to prevent life by blocking all communications and simply for that part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to fall, to be destroyed, or to bring the war to an end in one way or another. To come back to your question, surely everyone in the world must understand that the possibility to feed the population, for the population to survive is a key aspect of security. If you don't have food for your child, you will do everything you can to get food, even resorting to crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Mesic, as you spent the whole of 1992 in Zenica, in spite of such a dramatic situation as you have just described and the necessity which might even lead to crime, did both the military and the civilian police in those days invest efforts to find the perpetrators of offences, and are you aware whether they were prosecuted and punished?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you first that in this kind of situation that we -- that I have described, there were no inter-ethnic problems. People continued to live as they used to. Of course, the refugees had status of refugees. All the authorities, be they civilian or military, did prosecute those who resorted to crime as a means of resolving problems. I am aware of many trials that ended with very severe punishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in view of everything that you have described regarding the situation of the population and the large number of arriving refugees, did those authorities for law enforcement, that is the military and civilian police, did they have difficulties in identifying the persons who may have committed certain crimes? Were you aware of those difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know that very often investigating bodies were unable to find witnesses for the simple reason that there were none.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to my previous questions, you said that there were various pressures brought to bear on the population. Tell me, to what extent was propaganda a factor, and especially HVO propaganda with respect to developments in Zenica? Were you aware of problems resulting from such propaganda, and how did you deal with them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Propaganda was horrific. The goal of both parties was to move out the Croat and Serb populations from Zenica and to create conditions for a final division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They sought to achieve this in all possible ways, either using -- by using the media or by military activities in Zenica to cause fear among their people and prompt them to flee. Thus, for instance, in April 1993 a projectile was fired from Croatian positions which I think killed some 15 people, inhabitants of Zenica, who were in front of the city department stores. However, among the dead were both Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks, almost in the same proportion as the population. And this attack, in fact, was meant to give the message to the Croat people to leave Zenica and to join their ethnic group. This disastrous propaganda saying that all kinds of things were happening in Zenica designed to destroy one or another ethnicity was designed to move the population. So ethnic cleansing was the goal of both parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which parties you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Serbian and Croatian sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, Mr. Mesic, we were talking about Dusina, and now we're talking about propaganda. Let me quote just an excerpt from Prosecution Exhibit P649, where it says: "In the mixed village of Dusina, all Croat houses have been burnt, and there is massacre and terror against women, children, and the elderly. We don't have exact data on casualties, but we do know that 33 soldiers of the HVO were killed. How cruel the ABiH forces are is proven by the fact that all seven HVO members who took part in negotiations were killed." Did such an event ever occur in the village of Dusina, to the best your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Propaganda is a monstrous thing, and monstrous aims and conclusions are made dependent to -- designed to promote their goals. Such events never happened in Zenica, and civilians were never killed for any reason. How sick that propaganda is, I will tell you by saying that during a religious holiday in Zenica, it was said that a Catholic priest was hanged and Croats executed. This was published in June, July, but the real truth was that there was a very normal celebration there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we are talking about the events in April when you had the honourable task of bringing back a part of the population who had left their homes, can you tell me whether at that time there were hundreds of killed and slaughtered civilians and whether the Croats who were not killed were taken to the mine to work there, for labour purposes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you first that the conflict in Zenica broke out just after the events in Ahmici. I also have to tell you that the inhabitants of Ahmici fled to Zenica, and they brought with them horrific news. Such a massacre was never recorded in the history, and it was carried out through a very effective military operation in a very short time. So it was after this that the conflict in Zenica break out. But after those conflicts, not a civilian was -- not a single civilian was arrested or executed, nor did his -- tortured in any way that you have referred to. So civilians in Zenica were never systematically mistreated. However, I must say this under reservation of individual crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mesic, if what I have just said was contained in a document, you would say that it was monstrous propaganda; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I may have another 15 minutes of questions. No, I thought it was the time for the break. But we have a few more minutes, I think. Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Mesic, what was the attitude towards religious buildings and religious officials in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The relationship among people of different faiths is rather a complicated thing. In The Hague waiting for this trial, I read an interview with a Dutch artist who speaks about the monstrous death of the director van Gogh, and a direct consequence of this event was burning of a school and damage to many mosques. I have said who the people from Zenica are. Many had been exiled from their homes, totally uprooted in religious and cultural terms. In the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, more than a thousand mosques have been destroyed, many people killed. And with that backdrop, in Zenica, religious life of all three main confessions functioned normally. All three churches actually were operating throughout the war. But I must add the following: Around mid-1992, the Orthodox church was damaged as a result of Croat forces' activities, and within a few days, again following orders from the Presidency, units of the civilian defence, with the help of a unit of the BH army, repaired the damage, and it was never damaged again. The Catholic churches were never damaged and functioned throughout the war. The Islamic religious community also operated throughout the war. It had one mosque damaged by a projectile from Serb positions, but that damage was repaired too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell me whether you knew what happened with the priests from the church in Brajkovici.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Of course I know. All that happened to them happened in my presence. Those priests, after combat operations, were in their homes, and they were allowed to choose whether they wished to live, Brajkovici, Zenica, or somewhere else. As they expressed the wish to be in Zenica in the church of St. Ilija, which had very good living conditions, the priests of that church asked me to go and fetch those priests. So together with my assistants, I went to that church. We spoke to Franjo Krizanac, and we agreed on the way that we would transport them to Zenica. And we asked them what they wanted to take with then, and they told them what they thought was important for them. Those were paintings, books, and other relics that they needed for their services. After that, they were given a truck, and with my personal escort, they were taken to Zenica as completely free citizens, and they continued religious activities in Zenica. Occasionally they would visit their parish, and when the conditions were normalised, as far as I know, they returned to that parish. I don't know exactly when. They had complete freedom of movement as opposed to other Muslim religious officials who couldn't move. They were able to move freely. And I think they stayed in Zenica for about a year or a little less, but they were completely free.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, when you reached Brajkovici at the request of the priests of the St. Elias Church with your assistants from the staff, were you wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: According to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions, the civilian protection has its own uniforms and insignia which are common to the whole world, and members of the civilian protection never wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, did you have weapons on you at that time? Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: If I said that we were working in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, then the question is superfluous. We never had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that these priests from the church of Brajkovici went with you to Zenica. Tell me, were they accompanied or escorted or taken in by the military or members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The event I am describing, I was the only escort, and my associates.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, Mr. Mesic, whether on the road from Brajkovici to Zenica there was a situation in which those priests were held or, rather, were incarcerated in a school building?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. If I incarcerated them, then they were incarcerated, but we had a cup of coffee in the local commune building and talked to some people, and carried on our way to Zenica. So there was no stopover, and I didn't arrest anybody, nor did anybody have that intention.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After their arrival in Zenica, what was your relationship with the priests from the church in Brajkovici and with the parish priest of St. Elias Church, Fra Stjepan Radic, Father Stjepan Radic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, we had serious friendly relations, if I can put it that way. Let me put it this way: Those priests helped us provide the Croatian population with a sense of security for their continued life in Zenica. So by their very presence, they demonstrated that life in Zenica was possible. So it was very good. Excellent cooperation which enabled a situation to take place that wasn't recorded in the history of warfare anywhere. And this is what happened: During a celebration of the St. Elias parish, and this took place at the end of July or beginning of August, we on behalf of the St. Elias parish church helped to organise the opening of a large monument or sculpture of the Virgin Mary, and this was cast in bronze, several tonnes of bronze, in actual fact, and it was a costly operation. And the head of the parish came from Sarajevo to attend this ceremony. And it was also attended by representatives of the army and the police force and the municipal authorities, and it was a truly memorable event attended by several thousand people and their representatives. It was a wonderful event to be -- to behold during the war. And at the ceremony there were no problems. No incidents broke. And the statue of the Virgin Mary itself was never damaged in any way never broke. So, in a nutshell, my relationships with those priests were excellent and their position was excellent. Let me just say that Father Stjepan Radic, the parish priest, was a member of the official municipal delegation which visited a sister city in Germany, for example, and the name of that city is Bergen Kidilsch [phoen]. So Father Stjepan Radic was a member of the official delegation to travel to Germany and of course he testified about the people's needs in Zenica for food, medicaments, seeds for sowing for farming and so forth. So the relations was excellent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For me to be able to ask the next question, I would have to go into closed session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, may we go into closed session or private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, do you know Franjo Krizanac?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was he brought there in the identical manner or, rather, as you have described this in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was in my car with me, and there were two priests and two nuns.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the fact that Father Stjepan Radic was a very respected man and that just like you he, too, was a member of the official delegation of the Zenica municipality. Now, tell me this, please: All the Catholic citizens during the war, were they able to express and manifest their religion freely, and all the religious buildings in Zenica municipality, did they enjoy the protection of both the military and civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well me first of call say that Father Stjepan Radic was not only a highly respected priest but he also had some military recognition because the commander of a military brigade gave him this military recognition. Now, religious life in Zenica was more intensive than elsewhere, and in -- in wartime, people turned to God because it made their suffering easier to bear if they had the faith and believed in God. So religious life was completely public. It was not prohibited in any way, nor was it restricted in any way. And religious rites could be administered. All religious holidays such as Bajram, the Orthodox and Catholic Christmases and Easters were observed and celebrated with wide-scale festivities with the presence of other -- members of other ethnic or religious groups. So religious life evolved normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, my question to you, Mr. Mesic, is this: The prisoners held in KP Dom Zenica, did they also have the possibility of free access to priests or priests have free access to them so that they could voice their religious sentiments?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The prisoners of war, if I can say so, after the conflicts with the Croats, a whole unit surrendered and according to the Geneva Conventions, they were incarcerated but in institutions set for that, and it was the corrections centre where professionals worked according to procedure provided for the laws governing such institutions. So all these people, apart from the lack of food and adequate accommodation lived a fairly comfortable, if I could put it that way. They had the right to have priests visit them. How often, I don't know, but I do know that I myself went to visit some of my men with Father Stjepan Radic. Some of them were my friends. They were incarcerated, too, and nobody ever said that there was a problem of any kind. So given the prevailing circumstances, the maximum was done to ensure the right standards for these detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, today in Zenica are people coming back, Serbs and Croats coming back, people who left their homes during the war? And if they are coming back, what are your relationships? So this is a two-part question. Answer the first part, please. And second, when you did back to 1993 in your mind, can you tell whether you feel that you did everything in your power to reduce the war suffering to a minimum and to help people feel as safe as was possible under the given circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a complex question. People are coming back to Zenica, and I meet -- keep meeting friends who are coming back. They're coming back to their property, and to the best of my information, but let me say that I'm not working in the organs of administration -- haven't been working there since 1998, but I do know the situation. People are coming back, and they don't seem to be having too many problems to face in returning. But the dominant problem is unemployment, and Serbs and Croats are just as employed or as unemployed as the Bosniaks are. So this is a problem that we have to solve together in my municipality and my town. And another problem is the ironworks of Zenica to be operational again. And once that is done, then life will return to normal. But anyway, the powers that be, the local authorities are functioning on the basis of the population census in 1991. The parity ratio is being respected between the ethnicities. So if you would have an assistant of one ethnicity, his chief would be another one, and vice-versa. And the same is done in the cantonal administration where Serbs and Croats are being employed according to that parity key. Now, I myself have many Serbs and Croats who are friends of mine, and none of them, and they would tell me if they did feel some discrimination, but none of them seem to have any feelings of discrimination towards them. They are citizens of Zenica, one and all, and of course they face all the problems that the Bosniaks face as well. But I omitted to answer one of your questions, whether we were all able to travel. Only the Catholic priests could travel, and Orthodox priests, too, whereas Muslim priests were not able to travel anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the second part of my question. Is wasn't linked to the first part, but I wanted to make up for lost time. But what I wanted to ask you was this: When you think back to those events in 1993, do you consider that under the prevailing conditions at that time, you did your utmost? You took all the measures possible to facilitate the life of these people given the wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: My family origins don't give me the right to have bad thoughts any individual regardless of the ethnic group they belong to or the confession they belong to. That is something that my parents taught me at home, and that was the dominant principle that prevailed in Bosnia and Zenica. So we didn't have any ethnic problems there. I don't think I did anything special. I did what any other person would have done faced with the same circumstances. And when I see what is happening in the world today, I am happy to see, happy to remember what my town undertook in those war days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's ten to four. We'll be back at approximately quarter past four or 4.20. The meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the counsel for the second accused whether they have any questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no questions from us for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As soon as I hear "gospodina" said I know there are no questions. I turn towards the Prosecution for the start of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mesic. I have a few questions for you, and it shouldn't take too long. Let me ask you first, although you look very young to me, you haven't been born in 1971, on the 30 March 1971?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: 1951 is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 1951. Because that was what was recorded in the early remember transcript. Let me go to the events in Dusina. And you told us a little bit about, you know, that you were informed or somebody was informed by these local commissioners, and then I believe your assistant was dispatched with a team to Dusina. Let me just ask you a couple of questions about that. First of all, who is your assistant? What's his name?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: His name is the assistant for the sanitisation of the terrain, doctor -- I can't remember his name. But I'll remember in due course and tell you when I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. And who went with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Dr. Ilija Tatarevic. He lives in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, who or when was it the first time you personally got information about this Dusina case?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me about the exact date and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The information about the cessation of the conflict I got at the end of the conflict. If you're asking me about the time, I can't tell you, but fairly soon after the conflict ended. And at the same time, my assistant received orders to go and see to the sanitisation of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, on the day this -- your assistant went to Dusina, you did not hear yourself about what happened in Dusina. Somebody else informed him, and then he took off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No, no, that's not correct. All information in my staff went via me, through me, and I received the information from the Centre for informing. And if you with like more details, then the commissioner from the local commune informed the Centre for Information and Monitoring, the centre informed me in turn and then I took over my duties once I had received that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So my question again is: When did you personally receive information from this centre that something had occurred in Dusina so you could take appropriate steps? When did you receive information?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I received it immediately after I -- the centre had received the information, because we had radio communications once the conflict had ended. Now, what time of day it was, I really can't say, but it was as soon as the conflict ended, straight away, immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that would be the same day these events in Dusina, and I'm talking about the killings or the fact that these people deceased, it would be the same day that you received the information from the centre?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if these events occurred on the 26th of January, you would have received this information on the 26th of January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that I'm not quite sure whether it was the same day or whether it was the following day, but we acted once we had received the information after the conflict. I can't be sure whether it was the 26th or 27th. I can't remember. But of course that piece of information is something I have in my notes and documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where would these notes and documents be?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: In the Municipal Staff for Civilian Protection in Zenica and in the Centre for Monitoring and Information in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And they would still exist today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I assume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you know who your local commissioner was in Dusina who, I take it received or gathered that information and then passed it on to the centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact name now. I know the man, but I just can't remember his name just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know where he was stationed? Was it in Lasva? Was it Dusina? Was it in some other village?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: He's a resident of the Lasva local commune to which the village of Dusina belongs, so somewhere around those parts. But he wasn't in the combat zone, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you said that he radioed or communicated by radio to Zenica, and then you received it from the centre; is that correct? Because you just mentioned that you had radio communication, but if you can clarify whether that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he had radio communication with the centre for information. So I think that you should remind the witness of his question and not things that he didn't actually say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Please clarify whether that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on page 40, line 25, this matter of the radio. I took scrupulous note of it. He said there were radio communications one the conflict had ended, and I took note of that precisely. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So can you tell us with what kind of communication means the communication between the local commissioner in the Lasva area and the centre in Zenica the message was passed on?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every local commune had a radio station, and that radio station was used to inform the municipal organs and Municipal Staff of civilian protection about the needs and requirements of the local communities and a station like that existed in Lasva. The commissioner was duty-bound to report to the organ of the local commune, so they informed me. So I had a direct link and connection with the Centre for Monitoring and Information which in turn was connected and linked to the local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So what was the information you received about the Dusina events?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The customary information was the need for sanitising the terrain and no explanations are needed. A unit for sanitisation is requested, and the job is undertaken. So that's all that information would contain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it was you who told your assistant Mr. -- I think Dr. Tatarevic to go to Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us the team - I understand he wasn't alone - the team who went with him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The team was a simple one. There was Dr. Tatarevic with three assistants and a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you name us the assistants? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No, I can't, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were women among them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us more about these people? Were they young or older, experienced? Perhaps you recall, perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, since you're asking me, I remembered another name. Omer Subasic. He was a driver. Then there was Dr. Tatarevic. And I can't remember the name of the fourth member of the team. So it wasn't a team to carry out the actual sanitisation. It was -- they were in charge of the sanitisation whereas the local people actually did the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I understand from what you said just before the break that obviously these people aren't armed, but let me ask you, was that a dangerous assignment or was it a routine assignment to whom you dispatched this team?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: If you were in a war, then you must know that there are no routine assignments, because you can't foresee a situation. There's nothing you can do to guarantee security. It's always a life or death situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how long did it take for the team to return?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, the entire operation lasted several hours. I can't tell you exactly how long, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But they returned the same day?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, they returned the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you said they brought the body to the hospital, although you sort of phrased it in a general way that usually the bodies would be brought to the hospital. So let me ask you, did they bring bodies with them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. You say that one body was transported. All the bodies were taken to the hospital morgue. If I wasn't explicit enough, all the bodies were taken to the morgue at the Zenica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember how many bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: About ten. As many as were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you personally seen the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. Otherwise, I don't like situations like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where did you see the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: In the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it customary for you to go and see the bodies when a team comes back from the field and brings bodies to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: In fact, I saw the bodies first on the spot they were killed in, and in the morgue it was the professionals, whether the medical team or the investigating organs that examined them. Once we take the corpses to the body -- corpses to the morgue our job ended, and then we had work to do with the organisation of the funerals, burials, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if I understand you correctly, and I may not, did you say you have seen the bodies on the spot they were killed in?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No. You didn't understand me. Other instances, other cases I saw on the spot, but in this specific case I saw them at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So let me ask you again. Why did you go to the morgue in this instance? What triggered you to go to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I went to the morgue with the priest to discuss the details of the funerals and burials, the way that was to be done, because in Zenica during that period of time, there weren't enough coffins. So that's why I went to the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe to us the bodies you saw? Do you still remember the way they looked like?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't. Without wishing to sound insensitive, they looked like people who were dead. I can't go into the specific details, and I'm not the type of person that takes any pleasure in looking at things like that [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: For how long did you remain in the presence of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, because of the reasons I've already given you, it was very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember other people who were present when you saw the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think there's a problem in the interpretation. In line 23, page 45, it says they looked like dead people, but the witness added another phrase and said they had wounds, which wasn't interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can ask the question again, because it's quite true that in the English translation it says they "looked like people who were dead, I can't go into the specific details." So if he said he saw wounds, then there is a contradiction. So ask him to specify and ask the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. These wounds, could you tell us more about what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I saw dead --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer.
