utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I saw dead people who quite obviously had been killed -- had died from the results of firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether you saw other officials or civilians being present in the morgue concerned with those, I believe, ten bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: When I was there, the priest was with me, Markovic, Bozo Markovic, His holiness and my assistant Subasic, and one of my associates, Omer Subasic. And I assume that a family member was there, too, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was there an investigative judge or a policeman or somebody else there whom you recognised?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Not at that point. There was no investigative organ in that location, but it was customary that they complete their job by the time the bodies are brought to the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the people you just mentioned, for instance the priest, how come he was with you? Did you inform him or did he come on his own?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Previously I said that I had excellent relations with the religious officials, including the Catholic priests, and I think he came at my initiative and that we prepared for the funerals of those people together. That's why we were there together in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe that you said that you assumed there was a family member there as well, but I can't remember. Assuming there was a family member, would you also have called this family member, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I didn't call any family members. I came together with the priest to discuss procedures over funerals, and after that we contacted the families and organised the funerals. So this act went before all the other things we did later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in relation to these events that we're talking about, Dusina, did you have contacts with the police and/or the army?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: The way we work is this: We don't have any joint activities. Each of us has a separate part of the job to do. The police conducts the investigation. The army had completed combat, access was made possible, and a secure environment so that the army does its job, the civilian protection sanitises the terrain, and the investigative organs, the police and the others do their part of the job. So that was the situation in Zenica. But there the army didn't deal with sanitisation problems, although this wasn't -- because it wasn't regulated in that way. So each organ saw to their own field of endeavour. The police provided security and so on. So that would be the order of events, how things were done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you on this topic a related issue. You said before the break, and you were talking about these local commissioners, that there was cooperation with the army and the police. So let me ask you this: Do you know on what information the local commissioner acted? Who told him that there was something to sanitise in his area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: He received information as an immediate witness to the event. He lives there. So he was a witness of that military activity and the need to sanitise. And I assume that he was informed of the need to sanitise by the commanding officer of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Which would be an army officer?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: It should be an officer of the BH army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now returning to the morgue. At that time, did you know the identity of any of those ten bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I did not personally know their identity, but I was informed by my associates of some of the names, which I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On that day when you visited the morgue, you were told by your associates some of these -- the names of some of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you also told us that you received a report from your assistant, and we know now that's Dr. Tatarevic. Now, this report was an oral report or was it a written report?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The report was written. It was sent to me after sanitisation had been completed; yes, a written report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So the information contained in that report, and I remember two aspects that this was -- happened in the course of a fight of war and that the bodies were found in different places. That would be contained in this report?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This report, does it go to some institution, some authorities, or is it just stored and kept for eternity?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, the report -- it is my job to inform the Presidency and the republican staff of civilian protection about the events taking place in Zenica. Otherwise the organisation was such that the Information Services Centre would inform the republican civilian protection organ as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did anybody, any authority, police or military or security, approach you and ask about information you had in relation to these ten bodies? For instance, whether you or your collaborators knew about the circumstances of their death. Were you ever approached by somebody?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: It was customary for the investigative judge to work in the manner and procedure that he usually follows. He did not inform us about what he was doing, but after him we would complete our part of the job. In this specific case, we had no requests for additional information from the rest of the investigating organs belonging to the community or municipality or whatever. So we did not provide any information about the event to any of the investigative organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So I may have misunderstood you. The report Dr. Tatarevic compiled, did it go to the investigative judge or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: There was no need. We don't work according to the same principles. Dr. Tatarevic informs me about the activities undertaken by him and it is my duty to go up the vertical ladder and inform the Presidency or the republican staff. Only in exceptional circumstances if the investigative judge does not have sufficient information does he ask for our testimony, but that was on very rare occasions because the investigative judge worked according to his own procedure without having to resort to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now I understand and now -- thanks a lot. And in this case he did not ask you for additional information?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know on what basis your assistant, Dr. Tatarevic, made his two points, that this occurred in the course of fighting of war? Do you know whether he talked to people he encountered at the scene?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tatarevic nor any of my assistants, they are not investigating judges. They sanitised the land, they complete their activities, and inform me about the measures taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you don't know what the basis for his conclusion that this occurred in the course of fighting was? You don't know what his information was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't understood you quite. Dr. Tatarevic started his activities after the completion of the combat activities. He received information from the soldiers, so I don't know exactly what your question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. You just answered it. It was soldiers who told him what happened. That was the basis for his information?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not mention soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, it says in the transcript, but I can clarify again with your leave, Mr. President, what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you can just tell again what the source of information for Dr. Tatarevic was to say that this event happened in the course of fighting of war. Do you know, perhaps you don't, what the source of information for Dr. Tatarevic was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tatarevic need not know that there were combat operations. All of us in Zenica knew that there were combat operations because everything is close by. You can hear and see it. He didn't need to have a special explanation that there was combat. It is not his duty to make any assessments. I am the person making assessments and making decisions. Dr. Tatarevic is the person executing those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much for these clarifications. You told us earlier that, and I quote you, "Civilians in Zenica were never systematically mistreated." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we have heard evidence in this trial about a music school in Zenica. Do you know about the music school?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I know that there is a music school in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you hear about people being kept there and mistreated?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I heard of that event from a friend of mine several years ago, that apparently there was some sort of a prison there, but up until then I didn't know. That friend of mine was arrested and held in that prison allegedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The other point I wanted to clarify is you told us about all your efforts to bring the Croats back to their homes, and I commend you for all these activities. Now, there have been instances that Croat houses had been burned down; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your acknowledgement, but I said there was no systematic activity, but individual cases did occur. Crime is an unavoidable accompaniment to war. There was burning of Croat houses and Serb houses, but these were due to criminal activities by individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you told us that you are aware of many trials which had resulted in severe punishments. Were any of these people who burned Croat houses investigated and eventually tried?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: It is customary in police structures to conduct investigations against an unknown perpetrator. Such investigations were done. I don't know what the outcome was. I don't know whether any individuals were held accountable for burning houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I turn to the Defence for additional questions if they have any.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you heard about the music school from a friend of yours a few years ago. I will ask you, nevertheless, in 1993, did you have any knowledge of people being taken to the music school?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I did not know that any people were being taken to the music school. Had I known, I would have done everything I could to deal with the problem if it existed. I didn't know about it, and my feeling is that very few people knew what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on, you said that you were a friend with Stjepan Radic and other clergy and that you still have many Croat friends in Zenica. Did anyone ever, before this event a couple of years ago, tell you that he was aware of that problem or did he address you for your assistance?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No one ever told me about it, but my friends knew that I was the person you could address. And not just my friends but many other people in Zenica knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just two questions for today's witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of your friends that you mentioned who told you there was some sort of detention in the music school was called Franjo Togmacija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No, he's Franjo Tokmacija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tokmacija tell you that he was not mistreated in the music school?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: He confirmed that he had been detained there for a few days. After some activities in his town, and he comes from Kakanj, and that he was released a couple of days later and that he was not mistreated in anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a series of questions for you, but we'll start from the simplest to questions that will require more from your memory. A moment ago, answering a question from the Defence, you spoke of the insignia that you wore on your jacket, a badge that you are wearing. I understood that this was the badge of a particular political party. So could you tell us the name of that party?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is the badge of the Social Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you're asking me about this badge in my lapel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The persons working in the Municipal Staff of Defence, those persons who were working there, did they have to be affiliated with a political majority in the municipality or could they have also -- had a different political affiliation? In other words, the recruitment to the Municipal Staff at the time, was it political or was it based exclusively on professional ability? You should be able to answer that question, because I understood that you studied political science.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my case knows that people were not selected according to the party they belonged to but rather according to their expertise, and in all modesty I would say that I was a professional, too. I was the one selecting my associates and not political parties. To be quite frank, I was the only official in the municipality who was not a member of the ruling parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You were chief of the staff of civilian protection for Zenica municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you. I was the -- I repeat, I have to correct you. I was the commander of the Municipal Staff of civilian protection of Zenica. The chief of staff is subordinate to my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say you were commander, is that a reference to a rank or a position?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I mean the position. In civilian protection there are no ranks but only duties which start with the commander, the chief of staff, assistant commander, and the other personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your civilian protection service, did it belong to the municipal defence of Zenica? Your civilian protection service, was it integrated within what is known as the municipal defence staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: According to the law on defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the defence of the country consisted of the civilian defence and the armed forces. The civilian Defence covers all activities to ensure normal life and civilian protection. I think I've already said enough about civilian protection. So it was an independent municipal body that was accountable to the Presidency of the municipality, and it was not part of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your municipality, did it have within it forces which could, if necessary, lend a hand to the army?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: One of the obligations of the municipality is to ensure the functioning of the armed forces with resources at its disposal, and that applies to food, medical supplies, et cetera. Zenica municipality was not in a position to extend significant aid to the armed forces for the simple reason that it had to care for such a large number of refugees. So it was not able to provide resources to the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to show you a document, and you're going to tell me whether that document relates to the entity that you were subordinated to. Mr. Registrar, could you find Exhibit P210 in B/C/S. Will you place the document on the ELMO, please. You see that it is a document of a military nature. It's a document coming from the 3rd Corps addressed to the municipal defence staff of Zenica. Is this document addressed to the entity that you depended on? You're saying yes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No, no. I want to explain, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please explain. I'm asking you the question because I wish to clarify the point. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 3rd Corps Command in this document is addressing the Municipal Staff. Actually, I'm not quite clear who it is addressing itself to. Can I read the whole document before I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Can I answer now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: So I think that this is a document whereby the 3rd Corps Command is informing the Municipal Staff of Territorial Defence, which operated in all municipalities. Taken over from the previous political system of the former SFRY, the armed forces consisted of the Yugoslav People's Army and the municipal staffs. Those municipal staffs were operating for a while in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these were actually military bodies, military entities that were resubordinated to the republican staff of Territorial Defence. They had a staff of a regional character and republican staffs. They did not receive any commands from the municipality, nor were they accountable to the municipality for their activity. And I think that this document, in fact, was addressed to those staffs. It was not a part of the Municipal Staff forces, nor about the president of the municipal staff have control over these units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have seen the date of the document, the 23rd of January.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If try to understand what you're saying, this document was sent to the Municipal Staff of Zenica, which apparently something else and something different from the staff that you belonged to. What is the name of the person in charge of the OPSO in Zenica referred to at the top? To whom is this document addressed? Who is the person responsible for the OPSO of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have noted quite well these are two separate bodies. One is the civilian protection entity that -- and another is the Municipal Staff of Territorial Defence which was a military entity. It had its units. It engaged in military matters. And the highest official was the commander of that staff, who had a chief of staff, assistants, and other staff members. So this was a typically military organisation of a staff which was then called the Municipal Staff of Territorial Defence, but they had nothing to do with the municipality, nor could the Presidency of the municipality issue orders to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Municipal Staff of defence, as you call it, a military entity, what is the name of the person in charge of that staff.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Of course I can tell you. His name was Jasmin Saric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll now move on to civilian protection of which you were the commander. Above you, what is the name of the person who was responsible at the highest level?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, allow me to correct my previous assertion. I think at that time, it wasn't Jasmin Saric but, rather, Jozo Jerkic. One of those two persons was the commander of this staff you're referring to, the military staff. In Zenica municipality I did not have a superior. The commander of the republican staff was my superior in the chain of command, and I received instructions from the Presidency of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's the same one. So it's the same person. That is exactly what I thought I understood. So it's the same person. The person receiving this document is the same person as the one you depended on. Very well. We can take back the document. Let me pass on now to another question. Yes, the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I can be of assistance, but perhaps if the witness could clarify again -- at least I'm not entirely sure whether it's the same person. So if the witness could clarify it again. He talked about his chain of command. He was at the municipal level, and his superior was at the regional level, and he also had -- was given instructions from the municipality. I understand it's war Crisis Staff or the Presidency, but the document you showed, that was the Defence staff, which is a different body. That's my understanding. I just wanted to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us try and repeat. The document you have in front of you, I asked you who was at the highest level of the municipal defence staff of Zenica, and the name of that person. You first gave one name, Jasmin Saric, and then you said Jozo Jerkic. Was it the first or the second person, the former or the latter?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, allow me to explain, as noted by the Prosecutor. I'm afraid we have not understood one another at all. So if you wish let me repeat what I have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: We are talking about two completely different staffs. The staff in this document was a military body. It had its own hierarchy according to the law of the Armed Services. Its hierarchy was such that it had a regional staff and a republican staff. And that was the military hierarchy. In the municipal civilian protection staff, the hierarchy was is follows: I was at the horizontal level. I would be accountable to the Presidency of the municipality, and from them I with receive concrete orders, and also I could issue orders on my own if I felt it necessary to deal with problems for which I was responsible. Vertically my superior was the republican staff of civilian protection. And thirdly, the person who was in command of the staff on the 23rd of January, 1993, to the best of my recollection, was Jozo Jerkic. If I'm wrong, then it was Jasmin Saric. I can't remember exactly. One of those two persons was, but I think it was Jozo Jerkic, Jerkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Above him was there anyone else or was that the highest level?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I tried to explain to you. In the municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a command structure, there's always someone who has the highest authority. What I wish to know is the name of the person who was highest up in the hierarchy of the municipal defence staff of Zenica. That is my question. Who was at the top of the hierarchy? I'm not talking of the chief of staff but the name of the person who was number one in the municipal defence staff of Zenica referred to in the document in front of you. You have given us a name. Is that the name?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the Municipal Staff, Jozo Jerkic, or possibly the other name I gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now when we move on to the such protection of which you were a member. I'm trying to learn who was above you. You said that you referred to the Presidency of the municipality, and who was the president of the municipality? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to correct you. I reported to the Presidency, and heading that Presidency was the president of the municipality, and his name is Mr. Besim Spahic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So the president of the municipality was Mr. Besim Spahic. And the municipality, did it have at its disposal any effectives [as interpreted], civilian effectives which could assist the army?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The only forces that the municipality had at its disposal was the Civilian Protection Forces. There were bodies responsible for the mobilisation. They were part of the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll move on to another subject now, which is quite different from this one. You told us that you were at Grahovcici and that you brought back priests. You stopped in a cafe, and then you escorted them. Do you remember roughly when you went to see those priests that you brought back by car? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, this was -- I think it was the end of May, the day after the conflict at Ovnak. So to be precise, it was after the conflicts at Ovnak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were there, it was in what capacity? Was it part of your work? What made you go there? What prompted you to go there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I went there for professional reasons, and one of the reasons that could be outside that was the request of Father Stjepan Radic to assist in transporting his colleagues to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see much so you're telling us that Father Stjepan Radic asked you to go and assist in bringing back to Zenica his colleagues from the Grahovcici parish.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At the time, did you have a beard or did you look the same as you do now?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I looked much better than I do now, and I didn't have a beard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The persons you brought with you described the facts differently, and the Defence referred to that. They did not mention your name. We have the testimony about what actually happened, and it does not correspond to what you said. Are you quite sure of what you told us under the solemn oath, that is that you brought those people back in the car, that there were no military men, that you stopped to take a cup of coffee. Are you quite sure of that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What time did you go to bring these priests?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't tell you what time it was. It was during the day, and we returned during the same day. The whole thing didn't last more than a couple of hours. I didn't say that there were no military men there. There were no military men during their transport to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So on the spot, on the scene, you did see soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were soldiers nearby, and in the church itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, we're making some progress. So they were in the church. What unit did those soldiers belong to to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were wearing camouflage uniforms or traditional uniforms? You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: They were wearing the normal army uniforms, nothing special, of the 3rd Corps. Of the 3rd Corps. They wore the customary military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what makes you say that they belonged to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the checkpoint that existed at the separation line or on the front line. We passed through and were given approval by security organs of the 3rd Corps to evacuate the priests and the things they wanted to take with them. When we went there, the priests had a choice to go to Vitez, to stay in Grahovcici, to go to Zenica or somewhere else. What I asked them, and the security organ of the 3rd Corps or the unit that was there did not prevent it, was that if they didn't wish to stay in the church, did they wish to take something with them, and then they said they wanted to take all the relics they need for their work, paintings, crucifixes, books, and other relics that they need for the mass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were there. You were present. You were present when all this took place.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I was there all the time, and together with Father Krizanac, I assisted in getting his things ready and going to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you got into the car, there was you, yourself, and how many priests?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were no soldiers at all, no military personnel in the vehicle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: No, there was not a single soldier in the vehicle, nor did a single soldier stop us anywhere along the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you stopped, and what was the name you stopped to take a break and have a cup of coffee?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: We stopped in the local commune of Pojske, and that's where we had coffee, and it was a school, which was where the local commune was put up. And if you noticed the local commune is part of the local government. There was a clerk to see to the administrative matters and someone from the civilian protection staff, and in that building, on that premises, there were some other people who were there to deal with some problems they had, because that's where all the local problems were solved. When anybody had a problem, that's where they went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then you went to Zenica; is that right? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a relatively short drive. We chatted. I took them to St. Elias Church, and that's where they spent the whole time they were in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So how come the other -- some other witnesses said they were in the car and didn't mention your presence there at all? How do you explain that, this mission or the fact that they'd forgotten that particular fact?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you'd have to ask them that. But I feel hurt by that attitude of theirs, because afterwards, on several occasions after the war, I happened to see father Anto who was doing some work in Kotor Varos, and I went to see him during the summer and we talked. This summer actually. That was this summer and we discussed those events in a nice and proper manner and a good atmosphere and he expressed gratitude for what I had done. Of course I wasn't the only one and I wasn't alone in doing that, the staff did it. So -- also, on several occasions I visited Father Krizanac as well while he was conducting his religious services in the church at Guca Gora. And I'm very sorry to hear that, because I thought we were friends, and I'm sorry that they uttered the lies that they have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these religious people, the priests, took the solemn oath. Now, at line 6, page 1103, they stated the following: "In your cars, we were accompanied by soldiers." Shall I continue? Yes, I'm going to continue. "On the way, en route, we were stopped several times, and they asked us to get out of the car, but the soldiers did not authorise that." That's what they said under the solemn declaration, under oath just like you. So what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I say that is a complete lie for reasons unbeknownst to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And en route, did you pass through Ovnak?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what happened at Ovnak?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: There was an armed conflict between the HVO and the BH army at Ovnak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in the cars, without the soldiers, you arrive at Ovnak. Do you remember anything that happened in particular? Can you remember anything?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you arrived at Ovnak, I asked you whether you were in Ovnak. You said yes. So when you arrived there, do you remember what happened at Ovnak when you arrived? Nothing special?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I said that I remembered the event, but I have to tell you that the Civilian Protection Unit sanitised the terrain there, and what I remember is there were dead bodies there who Krizanac and I, that is to say father Krizanac and I myself at a later date buried in individual graves at Ovnak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the two priests say they were stopped -- that they stop at Ovnak and one of the priests recognised someone whom he knew, and he also said to him, "Osman, where were you?" You don't remember that if you were there? You don't remember this exchange?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we're talking about two different events. One was their transport to Zenica and the other is the burial of the people. What you're talking about now happened during the burial of the people, but you asked me about their transport to Zenica. So there are two different events that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you don't understand why they said there were soldiers whereas according to you there were none. We're going to take note of what you've just said under oath, under the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what your question is, what are you asking me? There were soldiers during that transport to Zenica, but nobody stopped us. That's what I claim. And all the rest is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see you're evolving now because now you say that during the transport to Zenica there were soldiers now. Is that what you're saying? And where were these soldiers, in the car, in another car?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat what I said. I don't know how it was interpreted, of course. I can't follow that. I said during their transport, that is to say from the time that I left, there was a conflict there, war going on, and soldiers were there, but soldiers didn't stop us on the way to Zenica at all. We just stopped in the local commune of Pojske that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the only question was to know en route when you went in the car the priests were surrounded by soldiers or not, or were there no soldiers? You said there weren't any soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I say there weren't any soldiers as their escort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. There we have it. That's what I was saying, line 6. They said on page 1103, they say otherwise, the contrary. That's it. It's twenty-five minutes to six. We're going to have a break and resume at 6.00. The Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the fact that a surname was mentioned of a protected witness on several occasions, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that half an hour will go by during the break so can we have the name of the protected witness redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, would you see to that and have the name struck from the record. We have 30 minutes for you to do that. We resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When we take up the proceedings I would just like to ask you one question and then I'll leave -- give the floor to the other Judges for their questions. I'm going to try through my questions to clarify matters regarding the transport of the two priests from point A to point B. You have already told us that you were present and there were no soldiers. The second priest who testified under oath, under the solemn declaration, just like you, said on page 1.004 lines 15. So it was I myself who asked him the question. I wanted to clarify the transport and I asked him a whole series of questions in that regard. And what I would like to do now is clarify the question of the transport once again. "Were you escorted," I asked the witness? And that is what the witness answered and I'm reading you exactly as the witness said it on line 15. His answer to my question was this when I asked him: "Were you escorted by soldiers?" He said: "Yes." And then he went to specify. "In the car behind each one of us there was a soldier with a weapon." Then I asked him: "Were you driving the car?" He said: "Yes. I drove one of the cars and my colleague drove the other car." And then he went on further to specify and that -- what he said was this: "And there were two nuns in the car and a neighbour -- one of my neighbours, a civilian." But he didn't give the man's name. So that might have been you, but that's it. So we had two witnesses stating under oath that that is what happened. And you have no recollection of presence of a soldier bearing a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the whole time from the -- there were -- on the area around the church there were soldiers, but when he started the transport there was not a single soldier and there was no car behind us with an army escort. I say under oath and I say with full responsibility that what I have stated is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, the second man when they arrived in Pojske, the locality of Pojske, contrary to what you said went on to describe and explain the following. He said he went to the school, not the cafe, where they came across parish civilians, people they knew. And once they had arrived there there was somebody who separated them. And at that point I asked the following question. I wanted to know who separated them, because if they were with soldiers who were bearing arms they didn't have freedom of movement. So he gave a name. He gave a name. And that is not along the lines of what you said. So you have re-asserted your testimony and we shall take note of that. I give the floor to His Honour, the Judge on my left who is going to ask you a question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness, I have a few, two or three, questions on what you said about the burial of the dead and the contacts you had with the families of the dead persons. I understood that together with the father Bozo Markovic you had contacts with the families and you also said this afternoon that none of the family members who contacted us discussed the cause of death of their family members. Is that a correct summary of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. You've understood that very correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So the two of you, Father Bozo Markovic and you, were in contact with these families. And my first question would be: Who of you was in contact with them? Who was speaking with them? Were you both speaking them? Was it you or was it only Father Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Bozo isn't a father of the Catholic -- he belongs to a different order, he talked to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But he is some kind of priest I understood. Am I wrong? He is a civilian like all of us. So Bozo Markovic and you, you had contacts with the family. Let me ask you again: Who had -- who contacted the conversations with them? Was it you? Was it him? Or were you both engaged in doing that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said in my previous answer that he went -- came into contact, not me -- contacted them, not myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you yourself had no conversations with the family members. It was only Bozo Markovic who spoke with them and he gave the information to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is in fact true because some of the families were not in the region of the Zenica municipality but in the Busovaca region. And His Holiness Bozo had contacts with the families and after that we organised ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So if you said, as you did this afternoon, none of the people who contacted us discussed the case -- cause of death, then this was some conclusion you draw from what Bozo Markovic told you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question properly. We didn't talk about the cause of death and I made the statement as I made it. I saw that the people had been killed from firearms, by firearms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: All right. I was just interested to know how this information or lack of information or absence of information on the cause of death came to you, but I understand that you deducted that from the silence of Bozo Markovic on the point. Okay. Were you two, were you on good -- did you know each other well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I knew the late Bozo Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Could you say that if he had heard something unusual about the death of these persons in Dusina in January of 1993 that he would have told you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I assume he would have because he wrote letters very frequently about some problems that he had in his parish and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: A different question is whether there was any discussion in Zenica on the events of the 26th with regard to the death of some ten persons. Do you recall any public discussion in newspapers or perhaps if there was on television? Or was it just not an issue?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Absolutely that was the top topic discussed in Zenica during those days. The stories ranged from the fantastic to the absolutely impossible and nobody had the real and proper information. But of course rumours and stories were going around, as you can imagine. The Presidency of the municipality set aside some resources, bought the coffins, which could not be had in the Zenica municipality at that time. So they were buried according to all the Catholic rites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Do you remember when they were buried? Was that a week later or some days later or immediate? Could you give me an indication, if you remember, of the date.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I have to say that the conditions in the morgue were not such that you could keep corpses for a long period of time. So they were transported and it was the Reverend Bozo who saw to that and they were buried and the funerals held. I can't remember the exact date but they weren't there for long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So a few days perhaps. Do you remember where they were buried?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember with Reverend Bozo in his parish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And what town or village was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: The Zenica municipality, the village is call Jedrenice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Were you present there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present at that funeral because I had other matters to attend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: A few days ago we had another witness who was telling about the events in Dusina and he said the burial would be a matter of some concern for public order and security. Apparently he expected that there would be difficulties or protests or I don't know what. Have you ever heard of that, that is this burial was something special, that there were public order problems?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: At the time the conflict took place in Dusina the Croatian Defence counsel of the HVO, as it's called, was a member of the Presidency of the municipality. Their president and member of the Presidency was Mr. Sakic, Mr. Dominik Sakic. And as to the affairs in Dusina and after Dusina he initiated a discussion that was held at the Presidency where it was decided that this event would not jeopardise public law and order and that the police and army were asked to put a stop to that kind of activity and to ensure that law and order was respected, as we like to say. So it was a high-risk security situation which the police forces monitored with all the necessary measures. So there were no problems and no unrest. Of course there were people who were dissatisfied, there were reactions of that kind of dissatisfactory at the meeting and Presidency level that were held, but law and order prevailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, this is what I wanted to know. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like one clarification. You said that Reverend Bozo Markovic, a priest, died. When did he die, that he is the late Bozo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Bozo Markovic died a few years ago, I'm not quite sure when, but let's say three or four years ago. Something like that. He died in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would the Prosecution like to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one clarification and I may have missed a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What religion did Father Bozo represent because I believe you called him His Holiness.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Well, you're better experts in Catholicism than I am. There are friars, or fathers, and we refer to them with "friar." Father Stjepan. And then there are the "Petrovcjijas," [phoen] we call them, a different order, and you refer to them as "reverend," actually not holiness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, reverend.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, who is Dominicans?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: They're the Dominicans in Zenica, the Dominican order, so they are addressed in a different manner. THE INTERPRETER: Interpreter's correction, it wasn't "holiness," it was "reverend."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So he was a Catholic, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, just a few clarifications. The President of the Trial Chamber asked you a number of questions linked to the structure of civilian protection and their relationship towards the military structures. I think that we have clarified most of the matters concerning this, but you said down the vertical chain your superior was the republican staff of civilian protection. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, that organ, was it a civilian organ like your municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a completely civilian organ, but I have to say that communication with that organ was reduced to technical exhibitions because Sarajevo was blocked. So they were brought down to basics through electronic communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in addition to these exhibitions I'm sure that you know that in 1992 the commander of the republican staff of civilian protection was Vinko Drinovac and in 1993 it was Kravic from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know who at that time was the commander, the supreme commander, if I can put it that way, who the President of the Trial Chamber wanted to ask you that question along the chain of command of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I'm asking you about the commander, the main staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina who was superior both to the corps and to the municipal staff of the territorial defence. Do you know who the commander of the army was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know who the commander for the army was. In 1992, or rather in 1993, it was Sefer Halilovic, General Sefer Halilovic, and later on General Delic. But the supreme commanders you asked me was the Presidency, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the main staff of the armed forces or the staff of the supreme command was a military organ quite different to the republican staff of civilian protection which is a civilian organ. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is completely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Sefer Halilovic as commander of the armed forces was somebody quite different than was your commander Kravic from Tuzla; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should just like to ask you one more thing. The witness [as interpreted] put parts of testimonies to you by witnesses in this court and read that in a car -- one car there was a civilian and that the car was driven by the priest. You at that point in time, were you the person driving the car or were you sitting in the back seat? Were you sitting behind the driver? I was driving Father Krizanac whereas Father Anto was driving the two nuns. There were no other people with us. Of course, my men were driving the truck carrying the goods we mentioned here. I, of course, do not know the reason for which these two men testified in the way they did. Because I say that Father Anto, Friar Anto, when we met this summer in Zup in the parish he is serving at the moment which is Kotor Varos, that's his parish, repeated his recollections and we revived our memories of those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify one point and with that I will terminate. The President showed you statements of two witnesses, or rather referred to statements of two witnesses, noting that they testified about what actually happened. Tell me, as you have been testifying before this Court under oath, did you describe the event of the transport of the priest from the Brajkovici church to the St. Elias church precisely the way it happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MESIC
utterances.text: Referring to my oath I declare with full responsibility that events evolved in the way I described them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, your testimony has just been completed. You have answered the questions of the Defence, of the Prosecution, and of the Judges. I thank you for coming to testify in The Hague at the request of the Defence. We wish you a safe journey home and I shall ask the usher to be kind enough to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 6.30, we still have a little time left. Are there any observations to be made? Any points? Any -- anything in connection with the planning for next week that we have already reviewed? I don't see anything. And the Prosecution, have you got anything to raise? No. The Defence has nothing. In that case, we will meet again after the weekend. The hearing will be resumed on Monday at 2.15 p.m. So we will be sitting on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday. On Wednesday there will be no hearings. Thank you. And we meet again an Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of December, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.31 p.m.,
